_doc: Harm between people: accountability after a mistake, abuse (yours or someone you know), and public allegations from all three seats. Every item carries a source that was fetched and read; anything the sources did not support was left out rather than guessed. Do not edit prose here without re-reading the cited source. Sections render on Learn beside consent.json.

accountability.title: Staying accountable
accountability.intro: The apology is the short part. Accountability is what you keep doing when nobody is making you. A lot of it happens away from the person you hurt. This is that part.

callout.title: If it is still happening, stop first
callout.body: It is very hard to take responsibility for harm that is still going on. So the toolkit's first step is to stop it.

groups.title: What it is, and what it is not

items.t: It starts with you, and sooner is better
items.d: Accountability is your own job. It is not something you wait to be made to do. The essay behind the four parts was written for small hurts and breaks in trust. For those, it says to say something as soon as you know you did it. Before they have to raise it. Waiting risks letting the hurt harden into resentment. They start building their own story, sometimes that it was their fault. You start building yours, that it was not that bad or it is too late. Needing to prepare first is often an excuse. The window for an apology can close.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability

items.t: It does not mean you get forgiven
items.d: The person you hurt does not have to forgive you. An apology does not settle it. The relationship does not have to continue. You may never be trusted again. They can always refuse an apology. They may not feel safe refusing it to your face. Someone who still feels in danger from you is not in a place to forgive. The Hotline says the path to forgiveness usually includes some accountability or changed behavior.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
National Domestic Violence Hotline — if an abusive partner apologizes

items.t: Sorry with a but is not sorry
items.d: Sorry, but you should not have made me angry, is not an apology. Sorry, but I never saw a healthy relationship, is not one either. The National Domestic Violence Hotline has a checklist of signs you may be hurting a partner. Blaming your anger on drugs, alcohol or the other person is on it. The toolkit's version is the same. Recognize the consequences without excuses, even where you did not intend them. What you did was a choice, not something someone else caused. Words have to match actions. A real apology does not end at the word sorry. Repeated sorries followed by the same behavior wear down trust. They wear down hope that anything will change.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — if an abusive partner apologizes
National Domestic Violence Hotline — am I hurting my partner?
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: Feeling defensive is expected
items.d: Thoughts like it is none of their business, or what about my side, are expected. The toolkit's advice is to slow down. To notice you are not going to be destroyed. It names the usual reactions: attacking back, withdrawing completely, or building your own camp of supporters. It says to find someone who supports you and challenges you at the same time. Someone who only agrees you were right is not that person.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: The four exits from shame
items.d: One research model names four ways people cope with shame. Attack yourself. Withdraw. Avoid or minimize. Attack others. It names a fifth, and calls it adaptive: admitting it and moving to apologize or make amends. Shame pushes people to hide, and to get angry and blame others. Guilt points the other way, toward owning it and undoing the damage. The model is a way to see which one you are doing right now.

sources.name: Tangney et al., Annual Review of Psychology (2007)

items.t: Which part was actually yours
items.d: Guilt about a specific thing has ways out. Change the behavior. Repair the damage. Apologize. If none of those is possible, resolve to do better. Guilt about a clear wrong is not linked to depression or anxiety on its own. It gets there when it spreads into shame about your whole self. It also gets there when you take on blame for things outside your control. So part of the work is being exact about what was actually yours. Not more, not less.

sources.name: Tangney et al., Annual Review of Psychology (2007)

items.t: Support has to come from someone other than the person you hurt
items.d: Changing what you do is the hardest part. It is easier with help. The essay's advice is to find people now. People you can talk to about your mistakes, shame and guilt. Before anyone calls you on anything. Harmful behavior is often part of a bigger pattern. A pattern takes more than fixing one thing. The person you hurt does not carry your accountability. Telling other people what you did counts as accountability in itself. Not to gather sympathizers. To stop hiding it, and to ask for help changing.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: The ways people slip out of it
items.d: The toolkit lists the common ones. Leaving the community or relationship to avoid it. Changing early, then sliding back once the pressure drops. Hoping people forget. Hoping people feel sorry for you. Blaming your past. Blaming the person you hurt. Making the process itself the problem. Insisting your version of accountability is the right one. It is a list to check yourself against.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: What real change looks like
items.d: The National Domestic Violence Hotline lists signs that an abusive partner is making real progress. Admitting fully. Dropping excuses and blame. Making amends. Not asking for credit for improvements. Not treating improvements as vouchers to spend on occasional acts of abuse. Not declaring yourself cured. Accepting consequences without self-pity or blaming others.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — is change possible in an abuser?

items.t: Some of it is not yours to control
items.d: Repair happens in relationship. You cannot do it alone. Sometimes it is not possible, because they do not want to engage with you. Seeing what you did, and changing, are still yours to do. If repair does happen, they choose how involved they are. From leading it to not being there at all. Your idea of what would fix it and theirs may differ. Some things cannot be given back. One of the toolkit's affirmations: offer the apology as a gift, expecting nothing back. Losing respect, standing, relationships, sometimes a home or a community, are possible costs of harm. The toolkit calls them costs, not punishments. Eventually you accept the losses you cannot control, and build self-respect anyway. If you share a community but were not close, the goal may be smaller. Just being in the same space without conflict.

sources.name: Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

notThis.title: Not a program that skips the point
notThis.body: If this was a pattern with a partner, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is specific. On their own, it does not recommend couples counseling or anger management. Nor substance-use programs or mental health treatment. It says they can sit alongside a certified batterer intervention program. The Hotline takes calls from people who think they may be causing harm. Not only from people being hurt. It says acknowledging it now is the first step. The number is under Survivors of abuse and violence in Communities.

abuse.title: When the person hurting you is someone close
abuse.intro: Some people are controlled through what they use. That has a name, and there are people who work on it. Nothing here tells you to leave. It is about seeing what is happening. Staying safer where you are. What to do if it is a friend.

callout.title: The drugs are not the reason
callout.body: Abuse is about power and control. Drugs are not the root cause. Getting sober does not by itself end it.

groups.title: What it looks like when drugs are part of it

items.t: Abuse is a pattern, not one bad night
items.d: It is one person keeping power and control over another. Hitting is only part of it. Threats, put-downs, control of money, being kept from friends and family. These usually come together. Early on the person can seem ideal, and the signs grow over time. Some from the National Domestic Violence Hotline's list: being told you never do anything right. Extreme jealousy about your time away. Being shamed in front of others. Pressure for sex. Pressure to use. Threats to kids or pets. Your things destroyed. Even one or two is a red flag. Anyone can be on either side of this.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — understand relationship abuse
National Domestic Violence Hotline — warning signs of abuse

items.t: Being made to use is part of it
items.d: NCDVTMH calls it substance use coercion. Its own list: being made to use, or use more than you wanted. Someone controlling your supply. Being put into withdrawal to get you to do something. Being stopped from cutting down or quitting. Being kept from a meeting or treatment. Being told you would be arrested, or lose your kids, if you called the police. Being told an assault was your fault because you were high. A yes to any one of these may mean it is happening to you. NCDVTMH also says this is not uncommon. A partner gets you onto opioids, then controls the supply. Then come threats if you try to cut down, get treatment, or call the police. Withdrawal, jail, losing your kids, or violence. Abusers lean on the shame around use to keep control.

sources.name: NCDVTMH — mental health and substance abuse coercion tipsheet (PDF)
NCDVTMH — substance use coercion, opioids, and domestic violence

items.t: It is common enough that people have counted
items.d: In 2012 the Hotline surveyed about 3,000 women who called. 27% said a partner had pressured or forced them to use, or to use more. Some had tried to get help for their use. Of those, 60% said a partner had tried to stop or discourage them. That was Hotline callers, and women only. It does not say how common this is for everyone. It does say you are not the only one.

sources.name: NCDVTMH and National Domestic Violence Hotline — mental health and substance use coercion surveys report, 2014 (PDF)

items.t: The calm after is part of the pattern
items.d: After a blowup there is often a stretch of apologies and promises. The person seems perfect for a while. The Hotline calls that a tactic. It keeps you there and makes you doubt it was really that bad. Gaslighting works the same way. It makes you question what you know happened.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — supporting someone who keeps returning

groups.title: Staying safer while you are still there

items.t: A plan is for staying, not only for leaving
items.d: You do not have to be going anywhere to make one. The Hotline says planning matters more when you live with the person. You cannot just walk out. Its advocates will build one around your situation, by phone or chat, any hour. The number and text line are in Communities, under Survivors of abuse and violence.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner
National Domestic Violence Hotline — create your personal safety plan

items.t: Things nobody else has to know about
items.d: The Hotline's list for people still at home. Notice how much force they use. It helps you judge the danger before it comes. Know which rooms have a way out and no weapons. Move there when an argument builds. Keep a phone within reach and know who you would call. Lock guns and knives away if you can. Have a few ordinary reasons ready for leaving the house. Keep the car backed in and fueled. Write down what happens. Decide now what you will do if it is found. If they have ever put hands around your neck, skip scarves and jewelry. Those can be used against you. If violence cannot be avoided, get to a corner. Make yourself small. Cover your head with your arms.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner

items.t: Let one or two people in
items.d: Tell a friend or neighbor you trust. Agree a signal they can see that means you need help. Tell them plainly who to call in a crisis, and who not to. Include whether you want the police. If kids or roommates are there, talk about how they get help. Agree a signal with them too. Ask them to stay out of the violence itself.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — safety planning while living with an abusive partner

items.t: Your head is part of the plan
items.d: Keep people around who are good to you. Pick one small step, like calling an advocate, with no promise to do anything after. Have a place that feels calm. If you keep a journal, keep it where they cannot get to it. It is not your fault. You do not have to decide everything at once.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — planning for emotional safety

groups.title: If it is someone you know

items.t: Ask, do not decide for them
items.d: Ask how you can help, instead of guessing. They know their partner, and what keeps them and you safe. Their partner already ignores what they want. One more person deciding for them does not help. The Hotline says not to stage an intervention. Ultimatums, calling the police, or trying to pull someone out can add danger. Heavy pressure can also mean they stop coming to you. That is what the abuser wants. Leaving and going back more than once is common. You cannot save another person. What helps: a place to talk without judgment. Ordinary time together. Being there whether they stay, go, or go back. You can say you are at your limit and point them to the Hotline.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — when a survivor asks you for help
National Domestic Violence Hotline — so you want to stage an intervention
National Domestic Violence Hotline — can I save them?
National Domestic Violence Hotline — supporting someone who keeps returning

items.t: Calling the police for them is not always safer
items.d: The Hotline says calling without their agreement takes away their say over their own safety. They may not feel safe being honest with officers, especially with the abuser there. Officers may not see what is happening. The abuser may hurt them more after the police leave. It is riskier still if the abuser has ties to the department. Immediate physical danger is different. Otherwise: ask privately what they need. Write down what you see, with dates and times. You can also contact a Hotline advocate to think through safety planning. A neighbor knocking on the door can interrupt.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline — should I call the police for someone else?
National Domestic Violence Hotline — when a survivor asks you for help

items.t: If someone tells you they were assaulted
items.d: RAINN's guide. Thank them for telling you. Ask what would help most right now. Listen without shock, blame, or why questions. Say you believe them and it was not their fault, as often as needed. Do not ask what they were wearing, or whether they had been drinking. Do not ask why they did not fight back. Or why they did not tell someone sooner. Never push them to report or get an exam. If they want a doctor or the police, offer to go with them. Keep checking in over time. There is no timeline for this. Your own feelings about it go to someone else, not to them.

sources.name: RAINN — how to TALK with survivors of sexual violence

notThis.title: Not a plan for leaving, and not legal advice
notThis.body: The Hotline says it plainly. The person in it has the right to decide if, when, and how they leave. Protective orders and custody differ by state. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you what applies where you are.

accused.title: If someone says you hurt them
accused.intro: Someone has said you hurt them. In person, in a group chat, or in public. This is what people who work on harm say about the first hours and after. It cannot tell you whether it is true. Nobody here can. The first steps are the same either way.

callout.title: Do not reach out to the person who named you
callout.body: They decide if there is any contact and when, and asking twice is pressure.

items.t: Stop before you answer anyone
items.d: You will feel a lot right now. Worry, guilt, shame, anger, the urge to defend yourself. All of that is normal. Take time before you reply to anyone. The pause is there so the feelings do not do more damage.

sources.name: DanceSafe — responding to and repairing a consent violation
DanceSafe — power dynamics, accountability and community response

items.t: Do not contact the person who named you
items.d: They decide whether there is any contact, and when. Not you. If you already asked and they said no, it stays no until they say otherwise. Asking again is pressure. Whether there is ever a conversation is theirs to decide.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)

items.t: Do not post your side
items.d: No rebuttal in the group chat. No list of what they got wrong. No saying they are lying, or asking why they are doing this now. That kind of reply tells everyone else who has been hurt to stay quiet. If you say anything, keep to what you remember of your own actions. Put the rest on a therapist, or someone completely outside the scene. If you are sure it is not true, that does not change the first days. One of these guides was written by someone who was named. Months later they were told the claim had no basis. They still say the same thing. No contact. No rebuttal. The needs of the person naming you come first.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)

items.t: Friends vouching for you does not help
items.d: People who love you will want to defend your character. Ask them not to. Ask them to help you look at what you did instead. Look for someone who can support you and challenge you at the same time. Not someone who only agrees that you were right. If you already have people like that, this is what they are for.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability

groups.title: What it does to your head

items.t: Feeling attacked is the usual first reaction
items.d: The accusation becomes the thing being done to you. You may feel alone in a sea of accusation. Furious that friends talked, or did not keep something private. Pulled to disappear, to gather your own camp, or to hit back first. Most people feel being asked to account as a rejection and a threat. Expect those pulls in yourself. Slowing down, and seeing that you will not be destroyed, takes real effort.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: Listening is not agreeing
items.d: You can hear their account without building your reply while they talk. Sit with all of it, not only the parts that do not match your memory. Let what they say add to your picture instead of erasing it. If you notice yourself wanting to defend or attack, stop and listen. Ask how you can understand more, not how you can defend yourself.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
DanceSafe — power dynamics, accountability and community response

items.t: Being hurt yourself does not answer this
items.d: Survivors can hurt people too. Saying you are a survivor too is not an answer. Neither is saying they have more power than you. It does not settle what you are being asked to face.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)

items.t: The fear is real, and it is not a punishment
items.d: People have lost friends, communities and jobs over this. That lands harder on people who already have less. Losing trust, standing, a role or a place in a scene are possible costs. They come from having caused harm. They are not punishments. Nobody can be made to like or trust you again, even if you change. One of these guides says facing the fear is easier than living in it.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)

items.t: It is a process, not one conversation
items.d: Accountability is not confessing and being done. It is practiced over time. Nobody can force it on you or do it for you. It runs on the terms of the person you hurt. It may include things asked of you: a program, some reading, stepping back from events. There is no timeline. It can take months or years, and may never feel finished. One toolkit draws it as a staircase. Stop the harm. See it. Own what it did, without excuses. Repair. Change. Become a healthy part of your community. There is no blueprint, and any step counts. There will be days with little energy. Plan ahead for what helps you recharge.

sources.name: TransformHarm — suggestions to people called out for abusive behavior (Clamor, 2002)
Mia Mingus — the four parts of accountability
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Taking Accountability (Section 4F)
DanceSafe — responding to and repairing a consent violation

items.t: If you share a scene, they lead
items.d: How you handle ending up in the same room is their call, not yours. What they need about contact and shared spaces can change over time. Being different now does not earn you access to them. It does not earn forgiveness. Using the process to push someone toward forgiving you is more of the same harm.

sources.name: TransformHarm — 9 ways to be accountable when you have been abusive (Everyday Feminism, 2016)
DanceSafe — responding to and repairing a consent violation

notThis.body: It is not legal advice. Whether contacting someone could break a court order or a law varies by state. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you. If you were the one hurt, the hotlines are in Communities. Look under Survivors of abuse and violence.

disclosing.title: Telling someone what happened to you
disclosing.intro: If someone hurt you, this is about telling people. Or not. Nothing here says you should. It is about keeping that choice yours, and staying safe once people know.

callout.title: You can think it through with someone first
callout.body: The RAINN hotline is listed under Finding your people. It never asks your name or location. It can help you decide if and when to tell anyone.

groups.title: Whether to tell, and how much

items.t: It is your decision, and only yours
items.d: You can tell one person, many people, or nobody. You never have to. There is no version of this where you owe anyone the story.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: You choose how much to say
items.d: A bare minimum is enough. So is the whole story. Being asked a question does not mean you have to answer it. RAINN suggests one line. You wanted them to know it happened. You do not want to share more. Some people push for details anyway. They ask if you are sure, what you were wearing, whether you had been drinking. RAINN tells them not to. If they do it anyway, that is on them. Not on you.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted
RAINN: how to talk with survivors
RAINN: how to help survivors heal

items.t: Waiting is normal, and so is never telling
items.d: Waiting to tell is common. So is never reporting at all. Waiting is not a sign that someone is lying, exaggerating or unsure. Never reporting does not make what happened less real. Fear can keep people quiet long after. Fear of being blamed, rejected or retaliated against. Some tried to tell earlier and were brushed off.

sources.name: RAINN: delayed reporting

items.t: How they react is not yours to manage
items.d: People you tell may get angry, confused, scared, guilty or shocked. Some may doubt you, hint you caused it, or say to get over it. None of that is rooted in the truth. What happened is only ever the fault of the person who did it. If you think they might get angry or violent, pick the place. RAINN advises somewhere public, or with someone you trust present.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: Some people are required by law to report
items.d: Teachers, childcare and eldercare workers, medical providers and some religious leaders can be mandatory reporters. If you are under 18 or over 65, they may have to report it. The rules vary by state. That is worth knowing before you choose who to tell.

sources.name: RAINN: how to tell someone you were sexually assaulted

items.t: If the person could find you
items.d: The basics, from RAINN and the National Domestic Violence Hotline: keep your phone charged. Save emergency contacts, under a different name if you need to. Memorize a few numbers. Change your routine and your routes over time. Tell people you trust what is going on. Agree on a code word that means you need help.

sources.name: RAINN: safety planning for survivors of assault, harassment and stalking
National Domestic Violence Hotline: stalking safety planning

items.t: You do not owe them a reply
items.d: Once you have asked them to stop contacting you, that is it. You do not owe a response. Replying tends to tell them their tactics are working. They may offer to stop if you meet in person. That is likely a way to put you at risk. You can block their numbers and accounts. You can change your number or email. Blocking can also prompt them to retaliate or make new accounts. So it is a choice, not a rule. Friends and family can block or report their accounts too.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline: stalking safety planning

items.t: Keeping records is optional
items.d: Saving texts, emails, voicemails and screenshots can help later, if you ever want it. For legal reasons or otherwise. The Hotline suggests noting dates and times. For some people it simply makes what happened feel real. RAINN says to save evidence only if you can do it safely. The Hotline suggests keeping it where the person cannot reach. A separate email account, or a trusted friend.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline: documenting abuse
RAINN: report and remove intimate images

items.t: Assume your phone and your posts are not private
items.d: A phone or computer can be monitored without you knowing. Browsing history is never fully erased, even in private or incognito mode. For anything sensitive, RAINN and the Hotline both suggest a safer device. A library, a shelter, or a friend's computer. And a new email account the person does not know about. Online, nothing is truly private whatever your settings. Deleted posts can live on as screenshots or server backups. You can ask people not to post about you or tag you. You can turn tagging off.

sources.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline: internet safety for survivors
RAINN: stay safer on social media
RAINN: safety planning for survivors of assault, harassment and stalking

items.t: If intimate images of you were shared
items.d: RAINN says the TAKE IT DOWN Act covers this. Covered platforms must remove them within 48 hours of a valid report. If a platform does not, you can complain to the FTC. StopNCII is a free tool for images of adults. It mainly works on exact copies, and only on platforms that take part. RAINN itself cannot remove images.

sources.name: RAINN: report and remove intimate images

notThis.title: What is not here
notThis.body: This page does not cover journalists, work or school. It does not cover the legal side of naming someone publicly. Those vary by state and situation. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you about the legal parts.

bystander.title: When it happened to someone you know
bystander.intro: You were not the one hurt, and you did not do it. You are the friend, the crew, the person they told. This is for that. Hotlines are in Communities, under Survivors of abuse and violence.

callout.title: Believe them. You are not the investigator.
callout.body: Believing them is a separate job from deciding what happens to the person named.

groups.title: If someone tells you they were hurt

items.t: Your job is to believe, not to investigate
items.d: Skip the shock, the blame and the why questions. Say you believe them. Say it was not their fault. Do not ask who it was, what they wore, or whether they were drinking. Do not ask how it happened, even out of curiosity. Those questions land as blame.

sources.name: RAINN — how to talk with survivors of sexual violence
DanceSafe — supporting sexual violence survivors

items.t: Do not push them to report, or to talk
items.d: Not to police, not to a forensic exam, not to say more than they want. Pushing can hurt them all over again. If they do choose to go, offering to go with them is enough.

sources.name: RAINN — how to talk with survivors of sexual violence
DanceSafe — supporting sexual violence survivors

items.t: Keep it among safe people
items.d: What they told you is not yours to pass on. Do not retell it as gossip. Do not post anything online that could show who they are, or where they go.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Supporting Survivors or Victims (Section 4E)
DanceSafe — supporting sexual violence survivors
National Domestic Violence Hotline — ways to support a survivor

items.t: Keep showing up
items.d: Support does not end after one conversation. Check in over time. Offer company, not pressure, and let them set the pace. Once attention turns to the person named, the one hurt tends to get left alone. Make sure it is someone's whole job to keep asking what they want. Do not make them ask for every single thing. Take your own feelings to a friend, a counselor or the hotline, not to them.

sources.name: RAINN — how to talk with survivors of sexual violence
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Supporting Survivors or Victims (Section 4E)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Some Basics Everyone Should Know (Section 2)

groups.title: If the person named is your friend

items.t: Check who you want to believe, and why
items.d: "They seemed so nice" is not evidence. Nice people do terrible things every day. That they were never like that with you proves nothing. Then look at yourself. Do you like one person more? Do you depend on one of them? Do they remind you of someone you like, so you want them to be innocent? Would you lose something by not taking their side? Challenging someone you care about can be a real way of standing by them.

sources.name: RAINN — how to talk with survivors of sexual violence
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Some Basics Everyone Should Know (Section 2)

items.t: You can care about them without covering for them
items.d: Being their friend does not mean excusing them or taking their side. It does not mean punishing or humiliating them either. It means helping them see what they did, stop, and take responsibility. Caring about them while supporting the person they hurt is not betrayal. If holding both is too much, take a smaller role or step back. That is allowed.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Mapping Allies and Barriers (Section 4C)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Supporting Survivors or Victims (Section 4E)

items.t: Watch for the usual moves, in you and in them
items.d: In you: shielding them from being held to account. Undermining what others are doing. Saying the person hurt was just as responsible. Calling the person hurt crazy. In them: leaving and hoping people forget. Blaming the person they hurt. Blaming whoever raised it. Making the process itself the problem. A friend can name these and stay, rather than join in.

sources.name: Creative Interventions Toolkit — Mapping Allies and Barriers (Section 4C)
Creative Interventions Toolkit — Some Basics Everyone Should Know (Section 2)

groups.title: If you are the crew, the house or the venue

items.t: Own your part instead of holding a trial
items.d: The person who did the harm is the only one responsible for it. The space still has a part. Name how it contributed, or let it happen. Change what let it happen. Support the person hurt. Support the process of holding the person named to account. Keep the changes going. You do not have to be at the center of it. Offering a room to meet in, or a ride, is a real role. You only need to know enough to keep it safe and private. If it is unfolding at an event right now, tell bar staff or security. They are trained for it.

Creative Interventions Toolkit — Working Together (Section 4G)
RAINN — bystander intervention, step in with CARE

items.t: Before anyone calls someone out
items.d: A call-out comes from the person hurt's own view of it, and from care. Canceling someone on the spot for a learnable mistake can push them away. Then they are less likely to change. Ask whether a call-in comes first. Ask whether they have done it before, and how much harm was done. Sometimes cutting someone off is what keeps people safe. Revenge, and shaming just to humiliate, are outside the model this section draws on. If your group wants different things, talk it through openly rather than acting alone. If you cannot see past getting even, a different role may fit better. Or stepping back for a while. A public response can also land on the person hurt as gossip, judgment and blame.

notThis.title: What this does not cover
notThis.body: Taking a report at the door. Banning someone, or canceling a booking. Wording a public statement. None of the sources we read cover those, so neither do we. Whether naming someone publicly carries legal risk varies by state. A lawyer or legal aid can tell you. RAINN's hotline takes calls from friends and supporters too.
